reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Usually arises as a complication of acute otitis media when infection spreads into the air cell system of the mastoid and pus fails to drain
Suspect it when a child with a middle ear infection develops worsening pain, fever and swelling behind the ear despite treatment
The classic sign is a boggy, tender postauricular swelling that pushes the pinna forward and downward, often obliterating the retroauricular groove
Otoscopy commonly shows sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall and a bulging or discharging drum
Progressive breakdown of the bony walls between air cells (coalescence) distinguishes surgical disease from simple mastoid mucosal inflammation seen in every acute otitis media
Contrast CT of the temporal bone defines the extent of coalescence, subperiosteal abscess and any early intracranial extension

Management combines aggressive parenteral antibiotics with drainage; cortical mastoidectomy is indicated when there is a subperiosteal abscess, no response to medical therapy, or a suspected complication
Pus should be sent for culture, and common organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas in chronic cases
reference.pathophysiology: The mastoid air cells are continuous with the middle ear, so mucosal inflammation accompanies most episodes of acute otitis media. Mastoiditis develops when purulent material is trapped because the aditus ad antrum becomes blocked by oedema, allowing pressure and infection to build within the air cells. Persistent suppuration decalcifies and destroys the thin bony septa between cells, which fuse into an abscess cavity (coalescent mastoiditis). Pus may then track outward through the cortex to form a subperiosteal abscess, along fascial planes into the neck (Bezold abscess), or inward toward the dura, sigmoid sinus and posterior/middle cranial fossae, producing serious intracranial complications.
additionalDifferentials: Severe acute otitis media without true mastoid coalescence
Postauricular lymphadenitis or infected sebaceous cyst
Suppurating postauricular lymph node from scalp infection
Furunculosis of the external canal with periauricular swelling
Histiocytosis or malignancy involving the temporal bone
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bone to assess air cell coalescence and abscess formation
MRI with venography when intracranial extension or sinus thrombosis is suspected
Otoscopy for sagging canal wall, drum changes and discharge
Culture and sensitivity of ear or abscess pus to guide antibiotics
Full blood count and inflammatory markers to gauge severity and monitor response
Audiometry once the acute phase settles to document hearing
redFlags: Headache, high fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting meningitis or brain abscess (intracranial spread is an emergency)
Swelling and tenderness over the sigmoid sinus region with swinging fever pointing to lateral sinus thrombophlebitis
Neck swelling and torticollis suggesting a Bezold abscess tracking into the neck
Facial nerve weakness or vertigo indicating deeper temporal bone involvement
Rapid clinical deterioration or failure to respond to intravenous antibiotics
reference.prognosis: With early recognition, appropriate antibiotics and timely surgical drainage the outlook is good and hearing is usually preserved, but delayed treatment allows intracranial and intratemporal complications that carry significant morbidity and can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Attributing postauricular swelling to simple lymphadenopathy and delaying imaging
Assuming any mastoid opacity on imaging equals surgical mastoiditis without correlating clinical signs and bony coalescence
Under-treating with oral antibiotics when parenteral therapy and drainage are required
Missing evolving intracranial complications by not reassessing the non-improving patient
Overlooking that the pinna is pushed forward, mistaking the picture for external ear pathology
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering common acute otitis media pathogens, refined by culture and sensitivity
Myringotomy with or without grommet insertion to drain the middle ear and obtain pus for culture
Cortical mastoidectomy for coalescent disease, subperiosteal abscess or failure to respond to medical therapy
Surgical drainage of a subperiosteal or Bezold abscess
Contrast imaging and urgent neurosurgical and ENT input for intracranial extension or sigmoid sinus thrombosis, with anticoagulation considered for sinus thrombosis
Audiometry follow-up once the acute phase settles to document hearing
